source.title: Practical Scaling Laws: Converting Compute into Performance in a Data-Constrained World

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures validation loss across model-size and training-data sweeps in its own experiments, but uses different model families, settings, and a running-min validation-loss measure rather than a direct reproduction of the original double-descent measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own validation-loss sweeps and explicitly states that it does not observe classical double descent. Its scaling-law comparisons and cited results are not rows; they are about predictive fit rather than the double-descent behavior itself.
record.test_reason: A scaling-law paper whose only engagement with double descent is a Limitations paragraph. Its loss is running-min (early-stopped) validation loss on coarse log-spaced size grids. The authors say this measure likely suppresses the model-wise peak and that the grid can miss it. So the measure cannot show the fall-rise-fall effect, and the stated non-observation is not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. In the Limitations section the authors state that their smooth asymptotic form does not predict a peak at N≈D and does not try to capture double descent. They say they do not observe it experimentally, likely because best-so-far validation loss suppresses the model-wise peak and the narrow peak range falls between log-spaced grid cells. The paper's main conclusions concern scaling-law extrapolation and cost-aware allocation, not double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper runs multi-domain scaling sweeps with several architectures and training recipes, using running-min validation loss for its main experimental loss surface; it is not an explicit replication of the original double-descent setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that running-min validation loss may suppress the model-wise peak and that the peak's narrow N range may fall between log-spaced grid cells. They also state that fitted scaling-law constants depend on architecture and training recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: Under early-stopped (running-min) validation loss, MNIST MLPs at D=60k reach a best loss near N≈250k. Larger models up to 74M params do worse, with no second descent visible on the log grid.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With optimal early stopping, best achievable validation cross-entropy at fixed data is U-shaped in model size rather than monotone or double-descent.

record.problems: The claim-relevant experiments report running-min validation loss rather than raw or final-checkpoint test error. The authors note that this can suppress a peak, and that their log-spaced model-size grids may miss the narrow interpolation region. The specific MNIST minimum is described as appearing around 250k, without an uncertainty interval for that location.

untested.parts: All: no final-checkpoint test error and no dense sweep around the interpolation threshold.
All: running-min trajectories cannot show a rise after a minimum.
All: no report of test error rising with more samples near the threshold.
All: no interpolation-threshold measurements in any model class.
All: no label-noise, multiple-descent or regularization-tuning comparison. Early stopping is applied by construction, never contrasted with no early stopping.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its challenges/limits_scope labels are not justified: the authors themselves explain the non-observation as an artifact of their measure and grid. Double descent is cited (refs 6, 38) only as context.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not resolve a dense sweep around the interpolation threshold; the reported experimental loss is running-min validation loss, not final-checkpoint test error.
The training trajectories use running-min validation loss, which cannot reveal a rise after an earlier minimum; the paper does not report raw test-error trajectories over epochs.
Although the experiments sweep unique-data size, the paper does not report whether more samples raise test error near the interpolation threshold.
The experiments span several architecture families, but do not densely test the interpolation-threshold peak and ensuing descent across model classes.
The paper does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, training time, and sample size.
The paper does not test label-noise dependence, multiple or triple descent, or whether optimal regularization removes a peak.
The paper does not test whether counting effective parameters turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: 2-hidden-layer ReLU MLP (MNIST)
rows.operation_detail: Measured running-min validation loss across model sizes in a model/data/training-exposure sweep.

conditions.value: 10 independent seeds per (N, D) cell; per-cell losses averaged before fitting

rows.measure: Running-min validation loss as model size varies
rows.value: The paper reports overfitting with increasing N and says N* appears around 250k for D = 60k.
rows.note: This reports a model-size minimum and subsequent degradation, but not the claimed fall-rise-fall sequence with a second descent.
rows.check: Running-min validation cross-entropy (best checkpoint), not final test error. The interpolation threshold is not located and the grid is a 10-point log sweep, so a second descent cannot be seen. The minimum near 250k followed by a rise is classical overfitting of early-stopped loss, not a V1 measurement. The value is read off a figure caption with no numbers.

rows.subject: Four training experiments: MLPs, PreActResNets, Fourier neural operators, and decoder-only transformers (aggregate statement)
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation-loss surfaces across model sizes in the four architecture/domain experiments.

conditions.value: log-spaced grids; the paper says the peak's narrow N range can fall between cells

rows.measure: Presence of classical double descent in experimental validation-loss results
rows.value: The authors state that they do not observe classical double descent in their experiments.
rows.note: The authors caution that running-min validation loss can suppress the model-wise peak and that the narrow peak range may fall between grid cells.
rows.check: An aggregate author statement from the Limitations section. The authors attribute the non-observation to their own measure (best-so-far loss suppresses the peak) and to grid spacing, so the measure cannot show presence or absence of double descent. Coding it as 'absent' and challenging V1/V4 is not supported.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
